blocks.heading: Key Concepts
blocks.html:
• Kidneys filter 180 L blood/day → produce 1-2 L urine
  • Nephrons: functional unit (glomerulus + tubules)
  • Glomerulus: filters blood (barrier: size + charge selectivity)
  • Tubules: reabsorb glucose, amino acids, electrolytes, water
  • Kidneys regulate: BP (RAAS), RBC production (EPO), Ca²⁺/PO₄
  • Acid-base balance via HCO₃⁻ regeneration

blocks.heading: Normal Values
blocks.html:
• BUN: 7-20 mg/dL (urea)
  • Creatinine: 0.6-1.2 mg/dL
  • GFR: >90 mL/min normal
  • Urine output: 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr
  • Urine specific gravity: 1.003-1.030

blocks.heading: What the Nurse Must Know
blocks.html:
• Creatinine is the most reliable indicator of renal function — produced at constant rate, freely filtered
  • BUN rises with protein intake, dehydration, GI bleed — less specific than creatinine
  • eGFR <60 for 3+ months = CKD; eGFR <15 = end-stage renal disease
  • Acute kidney injury: RIFLE criteria (Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, ESRD) or KDIGO

blocks.heading: NORMAL FUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Glomerular filtration barrier intact
  • Selective protein retention
  • Normal electrolyte balance
  • Adequate urine output with normal composition

blocks.heading: DYSFUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Glomerular inflammation → increased permeability → proteinuria/hematuria
  • Tubular damage → impaired reabsorption and concentration
  • Nephron loss → decreased GFR → uremia
  • Sodium/water retention → edema, HTN

blocks.heading: ⚠ Risk Factors (Non-Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Family history of kidney disease
  • Polycystic kidney disease (autosomal dominant)
  • Sickle cell trait/disease

blocks.heading: 💡 Risk Factors (Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Diabetes mellitus (#1 cause of CKD worldwide)
  • Hypertension (#2 cause)
  • Chronic NSAID use
  • Recurrent UTIs / obstructive uropathy
  • Dehydration
  • Nephrotoxic medications (aminoglycosides, contrast dye)

blocks.heading: 🔥 Complications
blocks.html: Hyperkalemia → cardiac arrest • Fluid overload → pulmonary edema • Uremic pericarditis • Metabolic acidosis • Anemia (decreased EPO) • Renal osteodystrophy
NRG Opposite: Kidney function impaired → filtration decreased → toxins accumulate + fluid/electrolyte imbalance

1. Glomerular injury: immune-mediated, infection, toxins

2. Increased permeability: protein and/or blood leak into urine

3. Tubular damage: impaired reabsorption, concentrating ability lost

4. Inflammation + fibrosis: progressive nephron loss

5. Decreased GFR: uremic toxins accumulate

6. Compensation fails: CKD complications develop

blocks.heading: Key Detail
blocks.html: Glomerulonephritis: immune-mediated inflammation of glomeruli → hematuria, proteinuria, HTN, edema. Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) → hypoalbuminemia → edema, hyperlipidemia. UTI: bacterial infection ascending from urethra to bladder (cystitis) to kidneys (pyelonephritis).

blocks.heading: Clinical Result
blocks.html: Decreased GFR → sodium/water retention → edema + HTN. Hyperkalemia from decreased excretion. Metabolic acidosis from decreased HCO₃⁻ regeneration. Anemia from decreased EPO. Renal osteodystrophy from phosphate retention and decreased vitamin D activation. Uremia affects every organ system.
NRG Sequencing: Each step leads to the next — understand the cascade to predict S/S and management

blocks.heading: Early / Mild
blocks.html:
• Fatigue, weakness
  • Mild peripheral edema (periorbital in mornings)
  • Nocturia (loss of concentrating ability)
  • Mild HTN
  • Foamy urine (proteinuria)

blocks.heading: Severe
blocks.html:
• Severe generalized edema (nephrotic), ascites
  • Oliguria (<400 mL/day) or anuria
  • Nausea, vomiting, uremic fetor
  • Pruritus, uremic frost
  • Hypertensive encephalopathy
  • Pericardial friction rub

blocks.heading: Hyperkalemia: peaked T waves, widened QRS, sine wave → cardiac arrest
blocks.html:
• Hyperkalemia: peaked T waves, widened QRS, sine wave → cardiac arrest
  • Pulmonary edema from fluid overload
  • Uremic pericarditis with tamponade
  • Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.20)
  • THIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY

blocks.heading: Diagnostic / Assessment Findings
blocks.html:
• Urinalysis: protein, blood, casts, specific gravity
  • Serum creatinine/BUN: elevated
  • eGFR: reduced
  • 24-hour urine protein
  • Renal ultrasound: size, obstruction, cysts
  • CBC: anemia (decreased EPO)

blocks.heading: Link Patho to S/S
blocks.html:
Decreased GFR → Fatigue, nausea, pruritus (uremia)

Proteinuria → Foamy urine, hypoalbuminemia, edema

Sodium retention → Edema, HTN, pulmonary edema

Decreased EPO → Anemia, fatigue, pallor

Hyperkalemia → Muscle weakness, cardiac dysrhythmias

blocks.heading: Cardiovascular
blocks.html:
• BP (often elevated)
  • JVD, peripheral edema (fluid overload)
  • Heart sounds (pericardial rub)
  • Weight (daily — fluid status)

blocks.heading: Respiratory
blocks.html:
• RR, SpO2 (pulmonary edema)
  • Lung sounds (crackles)
  • Work of breathing

blocks.heading: Neurological
blocks.html:
• Mental status (uremic encephalopathy)
  • Muscle strength (hyperkalemia)
  • Deep tendon reflexes

blocks.heading: Priority Actions
blocks.html: Daily weights and strict I&O. Monitor for hyperkalemia (ECG changes). Assess fluid status (edema, JVD, lung sounds). Protect vascular access (fistula/graft — no BP, IV, blood draws on that arm).

blocks.heading: Hyperkalemia & Vascular Access Alert
blocks.html: K+ >6.0 mEq/L with ECG changes = emergency: IV calcium gluconate (cardiac membrane stabilization), insulin + glucose (shifts K+ intracellular), sodium polystyrene sulfonate (eliminates K+). Vascular access: NEVER take BP, perform venipuncture, or start IV on fistula/graft arm.

blocks.heading: Lifestyle & Patient Education
blocks.html:
• Fluid restriction if ordered (typically <1.5-2 L/day)
  • Low sodium diet (<2 g/day)
  • Low potassium diet if hyperkalemic
  • Low phosphate diet + phosphate binders with meals
  • Protein restriction in CKD (0.6-0.8 g/kg/day)
🚨 Report Immediately: K+ >5.5 mEq/L | Oliguria <400 mL/day | Weight gain >1 kg/day | Severe dyspnea | Pericardial rub | Altered mental status

blocks.heading: Nursing Diagnosis
blocks.html: Excess fluid volume related to compromised regulatory mechanisms (decreased GFR) as evidenced by peripheral edema, weight gain 3 kg, BP 168/96, and crackles on auscultation

blocks.heading: Goal / Outcome
blocks.html: Patient will achieve stable fluid balance (I&O within 500 mL, no weight gain, clear lung sounds) within 48 hours.

blocks.heading: Interventions
blocks.html:
• Administer furosemide as prescribed — monitor response
  • Strict I&O and daily weights
  • Fluid restriction per order
  • Low-sodium diet education
  • Monitor electrolytes (especially K+)
  • Elevate lower extremities

blocks.heading: Rationale
blocks.html: Diuretics promote fluid excretion. I&O and weights are the most sensitive indicators of fluid balance. Sodium restriction prevents fluid retention. Electrolyte monitoring prevents life-threatening hypokalemia from diuresis.

blocks.heading: Evaluation
blocks.html: I&O negative 600 mL. Weight decreased 2 kg. Lung sounds clear. No peripheral edema. BP 142/84. K+ 3.8 (stable). Patient verbalizes fluid restriction.
NRG Care Plan Formula: Problem → Goal → Interventions → Rationale → Evaluation

What system is being tested?

Renal — filtration, fluid/electrolyte balance

What is the priority?

Fluid management + hyperkalemia prevention + protect vascular access

What is unsafe?

Giving NSAIDs to CKD patients, taking BP on fistula arm, missing hyperkalemia signs

What restores function?

Slowing progression (ACE-I), managing complications (EPO, phosphate binders)

blocks.heading: 💡 Key Memory Aids for RENR
blocks.html:
• Creatinine: Most reliable renal function indicator — rises with nephron loss
  • Hyperkalemia ECG: Peaked T waves → widened QRS → sine wave → arrest — ACT FAST
  • NEVER on fistula arm: No BP, no IV, no blood draws — causes thrombosis and loss of access
  • Proteinuria: First sign of diabetic nephropathy — ACE-I reduces proteinuria and slows progression
  • Fluid status: Daily weights are the single most sensitive indicator — 1 kg = 1 L fluid
NRG System Focus Formula: Renal Disease → Renal → Decreased GFR → Fluid/electrolyte imbalance + uremia → Priority: Fluid management + hyperkalemia prevention + slow progression

question.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min) is receiving hemodialysis via a left arm arteriovenous fistula. The nurse needs to obtain a blood pressure reading. Which action is correct?

options.html: Take the blood pressure on the left arm using a Doppler device
Take the blood pressure on the right arm with an appropriate cuff size
Take the blood pressure on the left arm but use a manual cuff only
Place an arterial line in the right radial artery for continuous BP monitoring

question.rationale: The absolute rule for vascular access (fistula/graft) is: NEVER take blood pressure, perform venipuncture, or start an IV on the access arm. This can cause thrombosis, stenosis, or rupture of the fistula, resulting in loss of the patient's lifeline for dialysis. BP must be taken on the contralateral (right) arm. Using a Doppler on the access arm is also contraindicated. An arterial line is unnecessary for routine BP monitoring and carries risks of infection and thrombosis.

why.html: Taking BP on the fistula arm can cause thrombosis and loss of vascular access
Manual vs automatic makes no difference — ANY BP on the access arm is contraindicated
Arterial line is invasive and unnecessary for routine BP monitoring
